claims.source: After learning spatio-temporal trajectories in a large-scale virtual city, subject-specific neural similarity in the hippocampus scaled with the remembered proximity of events in space and time.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI data analysis presented in the study.

claims.claim: The structure of the entire spatio-temporal network was reflected in neural patterns in the hippocampus.
claims.source: Crucially, the structure of the entire spatio-temporal network was reflected in neural patterns.
claims.evidence: This is a key finding from the representational similarity analysis.

claims.claim: There is a common coding mechanism underlying spatial and temporal aspects of episodic memory in the hippocampus.
claims.source: Our results provide evidence for a common coding mechanism underlying spatial and temporal aspects of episodic memory in the hippocampus and shed new light on its role in interleaving multiple episodes in a neural event map of memory space.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental findings showing similar neural patterns for spatial and temporal relationships.

claims.claim: The hippocampus plays a role in interleaving multiple episodes in a neural event map of memory space.
claims.source: Our results provide evidence for a common coding mechanism underlying spatial and temporal aspects of episodic memory in the hippocampus and shed new light on its role in interleaving multiple episodes in a neural event map of memory space.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observed neural patterns reflecting the entire spatio-temporal network.

claims.claim: The answer to the apparent duality in hippocampal function resides in a common mechanism required for both spatial navigation and episodic memory.
claims.source: It has been suggested that the answer to the apparent duality in hippocampal function resides in a common mechanism that is required for both spatial navigation and episodic memory (Eichenbaum, 2014): the formation of an abstract representation of the external world, a memory space (Eichenbaum et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work by Eichenbaum and colleagues.

claims.claim: The common mechanism for spatial navigation and episodic memory is the formation of an abstract representation of the external world, a memory space.
claims.source: It has been suggested that the answer to the apparent duality in hippocampal function resides in a common mechanism that is required for both spatial navigation and episodic memory (Eichenbaum, 2014): the formation of an abstract representation of the external world, a memory space (Eichenbaum et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This is based on theoretical frameworks cited from Eichenbaum et al., 1999.

claims.claim: Episodic memory has been defined as the ability to recall events from one's own life.
claims.source: Yet, episodic memory has been defined as the ability to recall events from one's own life (Tulving, 1983) in a specific mode of retrieval that has been referred to as recollection (Eichenbaum et al., 2007) or 'mental time travel' (Tulving, 2002).
claims.evidence: This definition is attributed to Tulving, 1983.

claims.claim: Episodic memory involves a specific mode of retrieval referred to as recollection.
claims.source: Yet, episodic memory has been defined as the ability to recall events from one's own life (Tulving, 1983) in a specific mode of retrieval that has been referred to as recollection (Eichenbaum et al., 2007) or 'mental time travel' (Tulving, 2002).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Eichenbaum et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Episodic memory involves a specific mode of retrieval referred to as 'mental time travel'.
claims.source: Yet, episodic memory has been defined as the ability to recall events from one's own life (Tulving, 1983) in a specific mode of retrieval that has been referred to as recollection (Eichenbaum et al., 2007) or 'mental time travel' (Tulving, 2002).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Tulving, 2002.

claims.claim: Humans must be able to convert relationships between events along physical dimensions of space and time into a mental representation.
claims.source: Notably, this implies that humans must be able to convert relationships between events, for example along the physical dimensions of space and time, into a mental representation so that the arrangement of events is appropriately reflected.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference from the definition of episodic memory as mental time travel.

claims.claim: Cells in the rodent hippocampus code for events in space and time simultaneously.
claims.source: In line with this idea, recent discoveries in rodent electrophysiology indicate that cells in the hippocampus code for events in space and time simultaneously (Kraus et al., 2013, 2015; Mankin et al., 2012) and provide evidence for the notion that memories are, in fact, stored in a multi-dimensional memory space (Eichenbaum et al., 1999; McKenzie et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to rodent electrophysiology studies.

claims.claim: Memories are stored in a multi-dimensional memory space.
claims.source: In line with this idea, recent discoveries in rodent electrophysiology indicate that cells in the hippocampus code for events in space and time simultaneously (Kraus et al., 2013, 2015; Mankin et al., 2012) and provide evidence for the notion that memories are, in fact, stored in a multi-dimensional memory space (Eichenbaum et al., 1999; McKenzie et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical and empirical work.

claims.claim: Memories are dynamically integrated into mnemonic network representations along different dimensions in humans.
claims.source: Findings from fMRI studies in humans also suggest that memories are dynamically integrated into mnemonic network representations along different dimensions (Collin et al., 2015; Horner et al., 2015; Kumaran and Maguire, 2006; Milivojevic et al., 2015; Preston and Eichenbaum, 2013; Schlichting et al., 2015; Shohamy and Wagner, 2008; Zeithamova et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to human fMRI studies.

claims.claim: It remains elusive how inter-event relationships along multiple dimensions are combined and converted into a multi-dimensional mnemonic event map.
claims.source: However, it remains elusive how inter-event relationships along multiple dimensions, such as space and time, are combined and converted into a multi-dimensional mnemonic event map, which might potentially support episodic memory.
claims.evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge that the study aims to address.

claims.claim: The hippocampus has traditionally been associated with the representation of space in rodents.
claims.source: In studies with rodents, the hippocampus has traditionally been associated with the representation of space (Burgess et al., 2002; Moser et al., 2008; O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978), i.e. knowing where events occurred.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational work in spatial navigation.

claims.claim: Place cells increase firing rate when a specific place in an environment is traversed.
claims.source: This spatial code is supported by specific neurons in the hippocampal formation such as place cells (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971), which increase firing rate when a specific place in an environment is traversed, and grid cells, which increase firing rate in multiple locations, organized in a hexagonal grid pattern (Hafting et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971.

claims.claim: Grid cells increase firing rate in multiple locations organized in a hexagonal grid pattern.
claims.source: This spatial code is supported by specific neurons in the hippocampal formation such as place cells (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971), which increase firing rate when a specific place in an environment is traversed, and grid cells, which increase firing rate in multiple locations, organized in a hexagonal grid pattern (Hafting et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Hafting et al., 2005.

claims.claim: Recent fMRI studies have pointed to similar spatial coding mechanisms in humans as found in rodents.
claims.source: Although much of this research has employed electrophysiology in rodents, recent studies using functional magnetic resonance imaging have pointed to similar mechanisms in humans (Doeller et al., 2010; Hassabis et al., 2009; Howard et al., 2014; Kyle et al., 2015; Vass and Epstein, 2013; Wolbers et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to human fMRI studies.

claims.claim: The hippocampus is crucial for episodic memory in humans.
claims.source: In addition to its role in spatial representation, the hippocampus is also known to be crucial for episodic memory in humans (Eichenbaum, 2014; Norman and O'Reilly, 2003; Scoville and Milner, 1957; Stark and Squire, 2000).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational work on hippocampal function in memory.

claims.claim: Episodic memory is inherently structured in a temporal manner.
claims.source: While it has been acknowledged that episodic memory is inherently structured in a temporal manner (Tulving, 1985), our understanding of the role of the hippocampus for remembering temporal structure has been limited for a long time (Howard and Eichenbaum, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Tulving, 1985.

claims.claim: Understanding of the hippocampus' role in remembering temporal structure has been limited for a long time.
claims.source: While it has been acknowledged that episodic memory is inherently structured in a temporal manner (Tulving, 1985), our understanding of the role of the hippocampus for remembering temporal structure has been limited for a long time (Howard and Eichenbaum, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Howard and Eichenbaum, 2015.

claims.claim: Situation-specific cell-assembly firing sequences have been described in the rodent hippocampus.
claims.source: Recently, descriptions of situation-specific cell-assembly firing sequences (Pastalkova et al., 2008) and the discovery of time cells in the rodent hippocampus (MacDonald et al., 2011) have sparked a renewed interest in the role of the hippocampus in temporal memory.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Pastalkova et al., 2008.

claims.claim: Time cells have been discovered in the rodent hippocampus.
claims.source: Recently, descriptions of situation-specific cell-assembly firing sequences (Pastalkova et al., 2008) and the discovery of time cells in the rodent hippocampus (MacDonald et al., 2011) have sparked a renewed interest in the role of the hippocampus in temporal memory.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to MacDonald et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Time cells selectively increase their firing pattern at specific time points after a cue had been presented.
claims.source: Time cells have been shown to selectively increase their firing pattern at specific time points after a cue had been presented, while animals were waiting to respond to an odor (MacDonald et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to MacDonald et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Time cells exhibited temporally coordinated firing pattern only in specific contexts.
claims.source: Interestingly, the cells exhibited this temporally coordinated firing pattern only in specific contexts.
claims.evidence: This is based on findings from time cell research.

claims.claim: Time cells show remapping behavior similar to place cells when context changes.
claims.source: In a new context, e.g. when delay time was prolonged, some of the previously responding cells ceased to fire or fired at different time points while previously unresponsive cells suddenly began to code for elapsed time, a response pattern akin to spatial remapping of place cells ('retiming').
claims.evidence: This describes the remapping phenomenon observed in time cells.

claims.claim: Time cells represent the specific temporal context of an episode rather than displaying a simple counting function or generic delay signal.
claims.source: Thus, rather than displaying a simple counting function or a generic delay signal, these cells seem to represent the specific temporal context of an episode, consistent with the temporal context model (Howard and Kahana, 2002; Howard et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This interpretation is supported by citations to the temporal context model.

claims.claim: Time cell findings have led to a re-examination of the hippocampus' role in temporal memory in rodents and humans.
claims.source: These findings have led to a re-examination of the hippocampus' role in temporal memory in rodents and humans (Eichenbaum, 2014; DuBrow and Davachi, 2015; Ranganath and Hsieh, 2016) and to several recent neuroimaging studies in humans.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to recent review and empirical work.

claims.claim: In predictable sequences, items that are closer together in the sequence elicit increased neural pattern similarity.
claims.source: For example, one study found that, in predictable as opposed to random sequences of items, items that are closer together in the sequence elicit increased neural pattern similarity (Hsieh et al., 2014), an effect which is dependent on the conjunction of item identity and order position rather than order position alone.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Hsieh et al., 2014.

claims.claim: The pattern similarity effect for sequential items is dependent on the conjunction of item identity and order position rather than order position alone.
claims.source: For example, one study found that, in predictable as opposed to random sequences of items, items that are closer together in the sequence elicit increased neural pattern similarity (Hsieh et al., 2014), an effect which is dependent on the conjunction of item identity and order position rather than order position alone.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Hsieh et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Items are represented differently within event boundaries than across event boundaries.
claims.source: Another study showed that items are represented differently within event boundaries than across event boundaries (Ezzyat and Davachi, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Ezzyat and Davachi, 2014.

claims.claim: Participants' judgment of temporal distance between item pairs was systematically higher when the pair was separated by an event boundary compared to when it was within an event boundary.
claims.source: Interestingly, participants' judgment of temporal distance between a pair of items was systematically higher when the pair was separated by an event boundary compared to when it was within an event boundary (even though the actual temporal distance was the same for the two types of item pairs).
claims.evidence: This behavioral finding is from the Ezzyat and Davachi study.

claims.claim: Behavioral judgment of across-boundary item pairs as being temporally close was associated with higher pattern similarity during learning.
claims.source: Further, a subsequent behavioral judgment of across-boundary item pairs as being temporally close was associated with higher pattern similarity during the learning task when compared to across-boundary items that were judged to be far.
claims.evidence: This neural finding is from the Ezzyat and Davachi study.

claims.claim: Previous temporal sequence studies investigated temporal sequences independently of the spatial relationship between elements.
claims.source: However, the temporal sequences in these studies were investigated independently of the spatial relationship between the elements.
claims.evidence: This identifies a limitation of prior studies.

claims.claim: Spatial and temporal aspects of autobiographical experiences are coded within the hippocampus across various scales of magnitude, up to one month in time and 30 km in space.
claims.source: Another recent report showed that spatial and temporal aspects of autobiographical experiences are coded within the hippocampus across various scales of magnitude, up to one month in time and 30 km in space (Nielson et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Nielson et al., 2015.

claims.claim: In the Nielson et al. study, participants wore a camera over four weeks that automatically took pictures throughout the day.
claims.source: Participants wore a camera over the course of four weeks, which automatically took pictures throughout the day.
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology of the Nielson et al. study.

claims.claim: In the Nielson et al. study, participants were scanned with fMRI while reviewing pictures and trying to recall what they depicted.
claims.source: Later, participants were scanned with fMRI while reviewing these pictures and trying to recall what they depicted.
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology of the Nielson et al. study.

claims.claim: The Nielson et al. study had little experimental control over stimulus material with regards to visual properties and degree of familiarity.
claims.source: While providing interesting insight into real-life autobiographical memory, there was little experimental control over the stimulus material with regards to visual properties and the degree of familiarity participants had with the locations.
claims.evidence: This is a critical assessment of the Nielson et al. study's methodology.

claims.claim: None of the previous studies compared changes in neural pattern similarity from before the acquisition of spatial and temporal structure to after.
claims.source: More importantly, none of the studies mentioned above compared changes in neural pattern similarity from before the acquisition of the spatial and temporal structure to after.
claims.evidence: This identifies a gap in prior research that the current study addresses.

claims.claim: An event map should be abstract to represent aspects of experience that go beyond a direct record of events.
claims.source: Abstract in the sense that it represents aspects of the experience that go beyond a direct record of events, such as being able to extrapolate that taking a specific turn in a city will be a shortcut even before the actual experience has been made.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical requirement for an event map based on cited frameworks.

claims.claim: An event map should be flexible to allow for representation of sudden changes in the world.
claims.source: An event map should further be flexible to allow for the representation of sudden changes in the world, such as roadblocks.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical requirement for an event map.

claims.claim: An event map should be able to represent relationships along different dimensions concurrently and conjunctively.
claims.source: Thirdly, it should be able to represent relationships along different dimensions concurrently and conjunctively, while still allowing to focus on one dimension depending on task situations, such as for example knowing that the spatial distance between two bus stops is short, but that it could take a long time to get to the destination during rush hour.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical requirement for an event map.

claims.claim: The study used a highly realistic first-person virtual navigation paradigm that led participants through a complex virtual city called 'Donderstown'.
claims.source: We used a highly realistic first-person virtual navigation paradigm that led participants through a complex virtual city ('Donderstown', see http://www.doellerlab.com/donderstown/).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claims.claim: 16 objects were arranged consistently in a spatial and temporal structure during the learning task.
claims.source: The purpose of this task was to provide a learning experience for participants in which 16 objects were arranged consistently in a spatial and temporal structure, defined through the complex network of inter-object relations.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claims.claim: The dimensions of time and space were dissociated through the use of teleporters.
claims.source: We dissociated the dimensions of time and space through the use of teleporters, requiring a high level of flexibility in memory (see Figure 1A for details of the task).
claims.evidence: This describes a key feature of the experimental design.

claims.claim: Objects were shown repeatedly in random order before and after the learning task.
claims.source: To ascertain maximal experimental control, the objects were shown repeatedly in random order before and after the learning task and all fMRI analyses were performed on data acquired during these independent scanning sessions.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claims.claim: All fMRI analyses were performed on data acquired during independent scanning sessions before and after the learning task.
claims.source: To ascertain maximal experimental control, the objects were shown repeatedly in random order before and after the learning task and all fMRI analyses were performed on data acquired during these independent scanning sessions.
claims.evidence: This describes the analytical approach.

claims.claim: Knowledge of the spatio-temporal structure was assessed with a memory test after fMRI acquisition.
claims.source: Knowledge of the spatio-temporal structure acquired during the learning task was assessed with a memory test after fMRI acquisition (see Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claims.claim: Participants' abstract representation of the event structure was estimated through all possible pairwise spatial and temporal distance judgments.
claims.source: Participants' abstract representation of the event structure was estimated through all possible pairwise spatial and temporal distance judgments, including judgments which required higher-order inference because events were separated by multiple intervening events.
claims.evidence: This describes the memory test methodology.

claims.claim: Distance judgments included judgments requiring higher-order inference because events were separated by multiple intervening events.
claims.source: Participants' abstract representation of the event structure was estimated through all possible pairwise spatial and temporal distance judgments, including judgments which required higher-order inference because events were separated by multiple intervening events.
claims.evidence: This describes a key feature of the memory test.

claims.claim: Participant-specific spatial and temporal distance ratings were used to investigate changes in neural pattern similarity using representational similarity analysis.
claims.source: The participant-specific spatial and temporal distance ratings from the memory test were then used to investigate changes in neural pattern similarity from before to after the learning task leveraging representational similarity analysis (RSA; Kriegeskorte et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This describes the analytical approach.

claims.claim: The study investigated whether increases in hippocampal pattern similarity co-varied with the remembered spatial and temporal event structure.
claims.source: More specifically, we investigated whether increases in hippocampal pattern similarity co-varied with the remembered spatial and temporal event structure during the learning task.
claims.evidence: This states the specific hypothesis tested.

claims.claim: Participants required on average 71.63 ± 13.75 minutes for the spatio-temporal learning task.
claims.source: Participants required on average 71.63 ± 13.75 (mean ± std) minutes for the task (range 52.67–113.06 min), showing high variability in navigation speed.
claims.evidence: This is a behavioral result from the learning task.

claims.claim: There was high variability in navigation speed during the learning task.
claims.source: Participants required on average 71.63 ± 13.75 (mean ± std) minutes for the task (range 52.67–113.06 min), showing high variability in navigation speed.
claims.evidence: This is observed from the range of completion times.

claims.claim: Navigation times during the last repetition were significantly shorter than during the first repetition.
claims.source: Navigation times during the last repetition were significantly shorter than during the first repetition (21.55 vs 11.60 min, T25 = 6.70, p<0.0001), see Figure 1—figure supplement 2 for more details.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data showing learning.

claims.claim: Participants were able to learn the virtual route.
claims.source: In sum, these data indicate that participants were able to learn the virtual route.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the improvement in navigation times.

claims.claim: Participants recalled on average 13.08 ± 3.06 of the 16 items in the free recall test.
claims.source: Participants recalled on average 13.08 ± 3.06 (mean ± std) of the 16 items.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the free recall memory test.

claims.claim: The order of free recall was more influenced by temporal order during the task than by spatial arrangement.
claims.source: The order of free recall was more influenced by the temporal order during the task than by the spatial arrangement, as assessed by correlating the spatial and temporal distances between items during the task with the distance in order during free recall (mean R for spatial distance: −0.01 ± 0.16 [mean ± std]; temporal distance: 0.50 ± 0.40 [mean ± std]; T25 = 4.32, p<0.0003).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the free recall analysis.

claims.claim: For temporal judgments, memory distances were significantly correlated with actual temporal distances in 24 of the 26 participants.
claims.source: For temporal judgments, memory distances were significantly correlated with actual temporal distances in 24 of the 26 participants (p<0.05; R = 0.64 ± 0.29 (mean ± std), see Figure 2A for the correlation coefficients across participants and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for participant-specific scatter plots).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the distance judgment task showing good temporal memory.

claims.claim: For spatial judgments, memory distances were significantly correlated with actual spatial distances in 21 of the 26 participants.
claims.source: For spatial judgments, memory distances were significantly correlated with actual spatial distances in 21 of the 26 participants (p<0.05; mean ± std: R = 0.49 ± 0.29); Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the distance judgment task showing good spatial memory.

claims.claim: Correspondence between actual and reproduced distances was very high for both space and time.
claims.source: Thus, correspondence between actual and reproduced distances was very high for both space and time and slightly better for the temporal than for the spatial condition (T25 = −2.52, p = 0.019).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the distance judgment results.

claims.claim: Correspondence between actual and reproduced distances was slightly better for the temporal than for the spatial condition.
claims.source: Thus, correspondence between actual and reproduced distances was very high for both space and time and slightly better for the temporal than for the spatial condition (T25 = −2.52, p = 0.019).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result comparing spatial and temporal memory accuracy.

claims.claim: In 14 of the 26 participants, there was a significant correlation between their spatial and temporal distance judgments.
claims.source: Indeed, we found that in 14 of the 26 participants, there was a significant correlation between their spatial and temporal distance judgments (p<0.05, R = 0.31 ± 0.29 [mean ± std]).
claims.evidence: This is a result showing that spatial and temporal judgments were not independent in some participants.

claims.claim: The two factors of space and time were not independent in most participants' memory judgments.
claims.source: Therefore, the two factors were not independent in most participants' memory judgments and we addressed this in our fMRI analysis (see below).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the correlation between spatial and temporal judgments.

claims.claim: Both actual spatial distances and actual temporal distances explained variance in spatial distance ratings.
claims.source: Across participants, both actual spatial distances and actual temporal distances explained variance in spatial distance ratings (beta for the factor actual spatial distance: 0.50 ± 0.28 [mean ± std], significantly different from zero across participants: T25 = 9.08, p<0.0001; beta for the factor actual temporal distance 0.17 ± 0.19 [mean ± std]; significantly different from zero across participants: T25 = 4.48, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a result from GLM analysis of distance judgments.

claims.claim: The factor actual spatial distance had a significantly greater impact on spatial distance ratings than the factor actual temporal distance.
claims.source: However, the factor actual spatial distance had a significantly greater impact on spatial distance ratings than the factor actual temporal distance (t-test between betas across participants for space > time: T25 = 4.06, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from comparing GLM betas.

claims.claim: Both actual spatial distances and actual temporal distances explained variance in temporal distance ratings.
claims.source: Similarly, both actual spatial distances and actual temporal distances explained variance in temporal distance ratings (beta for the factor actual spatial distance: 0.16 ± 0.22 [mean ± std], significantly different from zero across participants: T25 = 3.58, p<0.01; beta for the factor actual temporal distance 0.65 ± 0.27 [mean ± std]; significantly different from zero across participants: T25 = 12.16, p<0.0001).
claims.evidence: This is a result from GLM analysis of distance judgments.

claims.claim: The factor actual temporal distance had a much bigger impact on temporal distance ratings than the factor actual spatial distance.
claims.source: The factor actual temporal distance had a much bigger impact on temporal distance ratings than the factor actual spatial distance (t-test between betas across participants for time > space T25 = 5.33, p<0.0001).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from comparing GLM betas.

claims.claim: While there was some 'cross-over' between the domain that should be rated and the respective other domain, the domain that should be rated had a greater impact on the judgments both for space and for time.
claims.source: Thus, while there was some 'cross-over' between the domain that should be rated and the respective other domain, the domain that should be rated had a greater impact on the judgments both for space and for time.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the GLM analysis of distance judgments.

claims.claim: Errors in spatial distance ratings were correlated both with actual temporal distance and remembered temporal distances.
claims.source: Indeed, we found that errors in spatial distance ratings were correlated both with actual temporal distance and remembered temporal distances (Fisher z-transformed correlation coefficients tested against zero across participants; actual temporal distance: T25 = −5.39, p<0.0001; remembered temporal distance: T25 = −5.33, p<0.0001).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from error analysis.

claims.claim: Errors in temporal distance ratings were correlated with both actual spatial distances and remembered spatial distances.
claims.source: Similarly, errors in temporal distance ratings were correlated with both actual spatial distances and remembered spatial distances (Fisher z-transformed correlation coefficients tested against zero across participants; actual spatial distance: T25 = −4.82, p<0.0001; remembered spatial distance: T25 = −5.04, p<0.0001).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from error analysis.

claims.claim: The order in which spatial or temporal distances were probed did not have an impact on biases in the distance judgments.
claims.source: This means that the order in which spatial or temporal distances were probed did not have an impact on biases in the distance judgments.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the test order analysis.

claims.claim: Participants were mostly accurate in reproducing the spatial and temporal structure between objects that had not been directly experienced together.
claims.source: Taken together, these behavioral results show that participants were mostly accurate in reproducing the spatial and temporal structure between objects that had not been directly experienced together, indicating that they successfully formed an abstract, relational event map.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the behavioral memory test results.

claims.claim: Participants successfully formed an abstract, relational event map.
claims.source: Taken together, these behavioral results show that participants were mostly accurate in reproducing the spatial and temporal structure between objects that had not been directly experienced together, indicating that they successfully formed an abstract, relational event map.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the accuracy of distance judgments for non-adjacent items.

claims.claim: There is no evidence that either the spatial domain or the temporal domain had a bigger impact on distance ratings than the other.
claims.source: While spatial and temporal distance ratings were correlated with one another in some participants, there is no evidence that either the spatial domain or the temporal domain had a bigger impact on distance ratings than the other, and that the degree to which one domain was biased by the other did not depend on which domain was tested first.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the cross-domain bias analysis.

claims.claim: The degree to which one domain was biased by the other did not depend on which domain was tested first.
claims.source: While spatial and temporal distance ratings were correlated with one another in some participants, there is no evidence that either the spatial domain or the temporal domain had a bigger impact on distance ratings than the other, and that the degree to which one domain was biased by the other did not depend on which domain was tested first.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the test order analysis.

claims.claim: Participants positioned items with an average distance error of 0.193 ± 0.16 in the map test.
claims.source: On average, participants positioned the items with a distance error (expressed here as the ratio between the displacement error and the side length of the city map) of 0.193 ± 0.16 to the actual item location and performance was variable across participants (range 0.017–0.480, see Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the map test.

claims.claim: Performance in the map test was variable across participants.
claims.source: On average, participants positioned the items with a distance error (expressed here as the ratio between the displacement error and the side length of the city map) of 0.193 ± 0.16 to the actual item location and performance was variable across participants (range 0.017–0.480, see Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is observed from the range of error values.

claims.claim: Pattern similarity changes in bilateral hippocampus reflected participants' spatial distance judgments.
claims.source: We found that pattern similarity changes in bilateral hippocampus reflected participants' spatial distance judgments (Z = −3.719, pFDR=0.0005; FDR correction for 15 multiple comparisons, see Methods and materials), as well as their temporal distance judgments (Z = −2.597, pFDR = 0.0078), see Figure 5.
claims.evidence: This is a primary fMRI finding from the ROI analysis.

claims.claim: Pattern similarity changes in bilateral hippocampus reflected participants' temporal distance judgments.
claims.source: We found that pattern similarity changes in bilateral hippocampus reflected participants' spatial distance judgments (Z = −3.719, pFDR=0.0005; FDR correction for 15 multiple comparisons, see Methods and materials), as well as their temporal distance judgments (Z = −2.597, pFDR = 0.0078), see Figure 5.
claims.evidence: This is a primary fMRI finding from the ROI analysis.

claims.claim: Pairs of objects which were recalled as being close together either in space or time had higher pattern similarity increases across all hippocampal grey-matter voxels.
claims.source: More specifically, pairs of objects which were recalled as being close together either in space or time during the task had higher pattern similarity increases across all hippocampal grey-matter voxels.
claims.evidence: This describes the direction of the effect found in the hippocampus.

claims.claim: After removing variance explained by spatial distance judgments, residual pattern similarity changes still correlated with temporal distance judgments in bilateral hippocampus.
claims.source: First, we removed variance explained by spatial distance judgments from the pattern similarity changes in pairs of items in a GLM, and correlated the residuals from this model (i.e. what could not be explained by spatial distance judgments) with temporal distance judgments. We found that these residual pattern similarity changes still correlated with temporal distance judgments in bilateral hippocampus (Z= −1.805, pFDR = 0.041).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the control analysis testing independent contributions.

claims.claim: After removing the influence of temporal distance judgments, residual pattern similarity changes still correlated with spatial distance judgments in bilateral hippocampus.

results.result: The study employed a novel virtual reality paradigm using 'Donderstown' to create a spatio-temporal learning task where 16 objects were arranged with dissociated spatial and temporal distances using teleporters. Participants underwent familiarization with the city environment, then completed 14 repetitions of a route learning task, followed by pre- and post-learning fMRI scans during picture viewing tasks, and finally comprehensive memory testing.
results.evaluation: The experimental design is well-documented with clear methodological details (C47-C56, C180-C192). The use of teleporters to dissociate space and time (C49, C195-C196) is validated by showing no correlation between spatial and temporal distances (R = -0.0642, p = 0.4859). The familiarization procedure (C186-C192) addresses pilot observations about participant disorientation, demonstrating thoughtful experimental design. The pre-post comparison approach (C50-C51, C117-C119, C140-C144) provides strong control for confounds.

results.result: Participants successfully learned the virtual route, as evidenced by significant decreases in navigation time from the first to last repetition (21.55 vs 11.60 min, T25 = 6.70, p<0.0001) and maintained performance when guidance cones were removed in the 7th round.
results.evaluation: The behavioral data clearly demonstrate learning with appropriate statistical tests (C59, C193, C194). The lack of significant slowing when cones were removed (C193) and continued improvement thereafter (C194) provide converging evidence for successful route learning. The high variability in completion times (C57-C58) is acknowledged and does not undermine the learning effect.

results.result: Participants demonstrated accurate memory for both spatial and temporal relationships between objects, with 24/26 participants showing significant correlations for temporal judgments (R = 0.64 ± 0.29) and 21/26 for spatial judgments (R = 0.49 ± 0.29), indicating successful formation of an abstract relational event map.
results.evaluation: The memory test results are robust, with the majority of participants showing significant correlations between actual and remembered distances (C63-C64). The slightly better performance for temporal than spatial judgments (C66, T25 = -2.52, p = 0.019) is statistically supported. The conclusion that participants formed an abstract event map (C77-C78) is justified by the accuracy for non-adjacent items requiring higher-order inference (C53-C54).

results.result: Spatial and temporal distance judgments showed some interdependence in participants' memory (14/26 participants showed significant correlations), but GLM analyses revealed that each domain had a significantly stronger influence on its own judgments, and cross-domain biases were not affected by test order.
results.evaluation: The GLM analyses (C69-C73) provide strong evidence that despite some correlation between domains (C67-C68), each dimension primarily influences its own judgments. The error analyses (C74-C75) and test order analyses (C76, C79-C80) are thorough and appropriately control for potential confounds. The conclusion that participants could represent dimensions separately to some degree (C129) is well-supported by the statistical evidence.

results.result: Pattern similarity changes in bilateral hippocampus reflected both spatial (Z = -3.719, pFDR=0.0005) and temporal (Z = -2.597, pFDR = 0.0078) distance judgments, with independent contributions from each dimension after controlling for the other, and a strong combined effect (Z = -3.719, pFDR = 0.0005).
results.evaluation: The ROI analysis provides strong statistical evidence for hippocampal representation of both spatial and temporal distances (C83-C85). The control analyses (C86-C87) demonstrate independent contributions of each dimension, addressing the concern about correlated behavioral judgments. The combined space-time effect (C89) supports the integration hypothesis (C90). All results survive FDR correction for multiple comparisons.

results.result: Right hippocampus showed significant correlations with all five factors tested (spatial, temporal, combined, and each with the other removed), while left hippocampus showed significant effects only for spatial distance judgments and the combination of spatial and temporal distance judgments.
results.evaluation: The laterality analysis is clearly reported with appropriate statistical corrections (C91-C92). The differential involvement of left and right hippocampus is an interesting finding, though the manuscript does not deeply explore the implications. The statistics are sound and the pattern of results is internally consistent.

results.result: Searchlight analysis revealed partly overlapping clusters in right medial to anterior hippocampus for temporal distance (peak MNI:26/-18/-22, T25 = 4.05, pcorr = 0.0178) and spatial distance (peak MNI:34/-17/-22, T25 = 5.16, pcorr = 0.0046), with the strongest effect for their combination (peak MNI: 32/-17/-22, T25 = 6.07; pcorr < 0.0001).
results.evaluation: The searchlight analysis provides spatially specific evidence for the ROI findings (C93-C97, C102-C103). The control analyses (C98-C99) show that effects remain significant after removing the influence of the other factor, though slightly weaker. The overlap interpretation (C100-C101) is appropriately cautious, acknowledging both the correlation in behavioral judgments and the independent contributions. All results are corrected for multiple comparisons.

results.result: Objective spatial distances were associated with pattern similarity increases in bilateral hippocampus (Z = -2.85, pFDR = 0.02), but objective temporal distances and their combination showed no significant effects, suggesting a different pattern of results for objective versus remembered distances.
results.evaluation: The objective distance analysis (C104-C106) is methodologically sound and reveals an interesting dissociation from the remembered distance results. The ANOVA showing only spatial effects (C106) is appropriately reported. The interpretation (C107-C108) is cautious and acknowledges this as an interesting finding requiring future investigation. However, the lack of temporal effects for objective distances raises questions about whether the temporal dimension is truly represented or only emerges through subjective memory processes.

results.result: The study provides evidence for a mnemonic event map in the hippocampus where neural similarity scales with the proximity of event memories in both space and time, with both dimensions contributing independently and being integrated into a common spatio-temporal representation.
results.evaluation: This is the main conclusion of the study, well-supported by the convergent evidence from ROI and searchlight analyses (C109-C110, C158-C162). The claim of a common coding mechanism (C158) is justified by the pattern similarity findings for both dimensions. The interpretation that effects persist after controlling for the other dimension (C159) and the strong combined effect (C160) support the integration hypothesis. The conclusion about mapping the entire event structure (C161-C162) is supported by the use of all pairwise distance judgments including non-adjacent items.

results.result: The authors argue against an alternative explanation that effects are due to covert retrieval of visually similar scenes, based on: (1) nearby boxes not necessarily having similar views, (2) temporal effects occurring for spatially distant items, and (3) absence of significant effects in visual areas.
results.evaluation: The counterarguments to the visual similarity explanation are logical and well-reasoned (C164-C169). The point about teleporters creating temporal proximity without spatial proximity (C166) is particularly strong. The absence of effects in visual areas (C168) provides empirical support. However, this analysis could be strengthened by explicitly testing for effects in visual cortex and showing the results, rather than just stating no clusters survived correction.

results.result: The study introduces methodological advances including: (1) tracking de novo formation of event maps through pre-post comparison, (2) relating neural changes to participant-specific memory maps from comprehensive distance judgments, and (3) combining spatial and temporal aspects with teleporters to dissociate the dimensions.
results.evaluation: The methodological contributions are clearly articulated and well-justified (C117-C123, C130, C140-C145). The pre-post comparison approach (C117-C119, C140-C144) effectively controls for confounds like visual similarity and BOLD autocorrelation. The comprehensive memory testing (C120-C123) allows for participant-specific analysis. The combination of realism and experimental control (C130, C133, C145) is a genuine advance over prior work. These claims are supported by the successful implementation demonstrated in the results.

results.result: The study used a sample size of N=26 participants (mean age 24.88 ± 2.21, 11 female) determined by power analysis based on an effect size of d=1.03 from a previous similar study, with alpha=0.001 and power=0.95.
results.evaluation: The sample size determination is appropriately justified through power analysis (C177) using a relevant prior study. The demographic information is clearly reported (C179). However, the power analysis assumes the effect size will be similar to the prior study, which may not hold for this novel paradigm. Additionally, the gender imbalance (11/26 female) is not discussed as a potential limitation.

results.result: In the map test, participants positioned items with an average distance error of 0.193 ± 0.16 (range 0.017-0.480), showing variable performance across participants.
results.evaluation: The map test results are clearly reported (C81-C82) and show considerable variability. However, this test receives minimal discussion in the manuscript despite being one of three memory tests. The lack of correlation between map test performance and the main fMRI findings is not reported, which would be informative. The high variability (C82) suggests this measure may be less reliable than the distance judgment task.
